That vote won't decide the bill's fate outright, but it will be the clearest signal yet of whether the Senate can muster the 60 votes needed to move forward on final passage before the year runs out. Supporters argue the bill would finally give the crypto industry the regulatory certainty it has lacked for years, ending a period in which companies have often had to guess which agency's rules applied to them. Critics, including some lawmakers who otherwise support looser crypto regulation, argue the current text leaves major loopholes around conflicts of interest and DeFi oversight that could invite exactly the kind of abuse regulators are supposed to prevent.

The politics have grown more complicated in recent months amid scrutiny over crypto-related financial dealings connected to the Trump family, which critics say has made some Republicans warier of appearing to hand the industry a blank check, even as they remain broadly supportive of clearer digital asset rules. On the Democratic side, a handful of senators representing states with growing fintech and crypto industries have broken from colleagues pushing for stricter guardrails, arguing that continued regulatory limbo is doing more harm to consumers than a imperfect bill would.
What comes next

With the House already having left for a lengthy October recess and the midterm elections looming in November, the window for the Senate to act is narrowing fast. If the September 15 procedural vote fails to clear the 60-vote threshold, the bill's backers may need to renegotiate key provisions on DeFi and ethics protections to pick up enough votes from skeptics in both parties, a process that could push final action into 2027. Either way, the CLARITY Act's odd-bedfellows coalition has become one of the more unusual storylines of this Congress, a reminder that not every major fight in Washington breaks down along predictable party lines.

politics.title: Supreme Court deals Republicans a setback in Missouri redistricting fight
politics.dek: Justice Brett Kavanaugh rejected Missouri's emergency bid to revive a GOP-drawn congressional map, leaving the state's 2022 district lines in place for November and dealing Trump's nationwide redistricting push a rare loss.
politics.author: Amélie Roussel
politics.imageAlt: The U.S. Supreme Court building in Washington, D.C.

body.text: The U.S. Supreme Court on Tuesday declined to revive a Republican-drawn congressional map in Missouri, leaving the state's older district lines in place for November's midterms and dealing a real setback to President Trump's broader campaign to redraw House boundaries in the GOP's favor before the 2026 elections.

The decision came from Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who oversees emergency appeals from that part of the country. He rejected Missouri's request without referring the matter to the full nine-member Court and without explaining his reasoning, a move that leaves Missouri's 2022 congressional map, drawn after the last census, in effect for this year's general election.
What we know so far

The fight traces back to a special legislative session Missouri Republicans held in 2025 at Trump's urging, redrawing the state's eight congressional districts specifically to target longtime Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver's Kansas City-based 5th District. The new lines split Kansas City along Troost Avenue, a street Cleaver said had historically divided Black and white residents, shifting large portions of his district into seats held by Republican Reps. Mark Alford and Sam Graves. The redrawn map would have given Republicans a shot at winning seven of Missouri's eight congressional seats instead of six, and it was already used once, in the state's August primary election.

Opponents fought back through the ballot box rather than the courtroom at first, gathering more than 300,000 signatures for a referendum that would let Missouri voters decide the new map's fate directly. Missouri's Republican secretary of state initially rejected that petition, arguing redistricting couldn't be put to a public vote, and a lower court agreed. But the Missouri Supreme Court unanimously reversed that decision on September 3, ruling the referendum was valid and ordering the state to use its pre-existing 2022 map for November while the new plan goes before voters as a ballot measure.
A whiplash week in the courts

Missouri's attorney general moved almost immediately to challenge the state court's ruling, and a federal district judge appointed by Trump briefly sided with Republicans, ordering the new map be used after all. But that order was only ever meant to hold for two weeks while the dispute worked its way up, and Tuesday's Supreme Court decision effectively ended that brief reprieve, restoring the Missouri Supreme Court's ruling and, with it, the older district lines.

The stakes extend well beyond Missouri. Republicans currently hold a razor-thin House majority, and Democrats need to flip just a handful of seats nationwide to retake control. Missouri had been one piece of a broader, multi-state push, alongside Texas and other GOP-controlled states, to redraw district lines mid-decade specifically to protect that majority. Missouri voters will now get the final say themselves, deciding on the new map as a ballot referendum in November; if they approve it, the GOP-favorable boundaries could take effect starting with the 2028 elections, and if they reject it, the current map stays in place.

politics.title: Republicans open first-ever midterm convention in Dallas as Trump looks to rally the base
politics.dek: Trump and JD Vance headline a two-day, first-of-its-kind party convention in Dallas this week, an unusual midterm-year gathering aimed at firing up GOP voters as the party defends razor-thin majorities in a difficult political climate.
politics.author: Amélie Roussel
politics.imageAlt: The American Airlines Center in Dallas prepared for the 2026 Republican Midterm Convention

body.text: Republicans are gathering in Dallas this week for something the party has never done before: a full-scale national convention held in a midterm election year, without a nomination on the line. The two-day event, running Wednesday and Thursday at the American Airlines Center, has been nicknamed "Trumpapalooza" by some GOP leaders, and it's built entirely around speeches, fundraising and rallying supporters ahead of November, rather than the traditional business of choosing a presidential nominee.

President Trump announced the convention back in June, calling it a "truly Historic Event" in a Truth Social post and promising it would showcase, in his words, hardworking Americans, entrepreneurs and job creators powering what he's branded the country's Golden Age. The Republican National Committee has since released a full programming schedule packed with 109 speakers across the two days, organized around the issues national Republicans plan to run on this fall: lowering costs, securing the border, strengthening domestic energy and manufacturing, and other core planks of what RNC Chairman Joe Gruters has called the party's Common Sense Revolution.
What we know so far

Vice President JD Vance delivers the keynote address on the convention's first night, with Trump speaking on both evenings and closing out the event Thursday. The broader lineup includes Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., House Speaker Mike Johnson, and Republican candidates from some of the country's most competitive House and Senate races, all sharing a stage built to energize the party's base heading into an election where Trump himself isn't on the ballot but his agenda very much is.

Organizers expect roughly 20,000 attendees at the arena, which is why Dallas beat out nearby Fort Worth's smaller Dickies Arena for hosting rights. The choice of Texas as the backdrop is deliberate. The state sits at the center of this year's fight for congressional control, with several competitive House races and a marquee Senate contest where Republican Ken Paxton faces Democrat James Talarico in a race most analysts now rate a toss-up, an unusually close contest for a state Republicans have carried in every statewide election for three decades.
A rally against a difficult backdrop

The timing isn't incidental either. Republicans are defending narrow majorities in both the House and Senate against a historical pattern in which the president's party typically loses ground in midterm elections, and Trump's approval rating, including in Texas itself, has softened since his 2024 win. Party organizers are framing the convention as a direct answer to that headwind: a chance to put GOP accomplishments and candidates in front of a national audience before voters start making up their minds in earnest this fall, rather than ceding the pre-election narrative to Democrats.

Whether the gathering moves the needle in November remains an open question. But as a first-of-its-kind event in modern American politics, the Dallas convention is itself a marker of how unusual this election cycle has become, with a sitting president staging what amounts to a national rally months before ballots are even cast, betting that spectacle and star power can help offset a genuinely difficult political environment for his party.

politics.title: US-Canada trade war escalates as Trump bans dairy, alcohol and motorcycle imports
politics.dek: The Trump administration moved to block a wide range of Canadian goods hours after Ottawa's own retaliatory tariffs on $20 billion of American products took effect, deepening a rift between two of the world's most closely integrated economies.
politics.author: Amélie Roussel
politics.imageAlt: Trucks crossing the Gordie Howe International Bridge between Windsor, Ontario, and Detroit, Michigan

body.text: The trade war between the United States and Canada took a sharp turn Tuesday, as the White House announced it would ban imports of Canadian dairy products, most alcoholic beverages and motorcycles, just hours after Canada's own retaliatory tariffs on roughly $20 billion worth of American goods took effect at midnight. The dueling measures mark the most significant escalation yet between two countries that have spent decades building some of the most closely integrated supply chains in the world.

Canada's retaliatory tariffs, ranging from 15% to 50%, now apply to hundreds of American products including steel, aluminum, dairy, household appliances, clothing and farm equipment, matching the United States roughly dollar-for-dollar after Washington imposed 50% duties on about $20 billion in Canadian goods late last month. Prime Minister Mark Carney had signaled the retaliation was coming after weeks of negotiations between the two governments collapsed.
What we know so far

The Trump administration's response went further than simply matching Canada's tariffs. Rather than raising the cost of the targeted Canadian goods, the new U.S. measures effectively cut off American market access for them entirely, using authority under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, a provision that allows a president to bar imports from countries found to be discriminating against U.S. commerce. The bans on Canadian dairy products, most alcoholic beverages and large motorcycles take effect September 29. President Trump also directed the General Services Administration to declare Canadian products ineligible for long-term U.S. government contracts until Canada offers what officials described as "full and fair reciprocity" for American goods.

The dispute carries real political weight beyond the two countries' trade ledgers. The affected industries and supply chains touch swing states like Michigan and Ohio, both of which have competitive congressional races that will help decide control of the U.S. House this November. Trump is already navigating voter frustration over the broader economy and rising energy prices tied to conflict in the Middle East, and an intensifying trade fight with one of America's largest trading partners adds another variable heading into the midterms.
Where things go from here

Both sides have kept a line of communication open even as the measures escalate. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer has been in contact with Dominic LeBlanc, Canada's minister responsible for trade with the United States, and officials say the two are expected to speak again in the coming days to explore whether an alternative path exists. For now, though, both governments are publicly standing firm. Carney told Canadians in a video message that the country has "everything we need to pivot and prosper," while acknowledging the shift away from reliance on the U.S. market "will come at a cost." A separate, previously announced increase in U.S. tariffs on Canadian autos, from 25% to 50%, is still scheduled to take effect January 1, leaving open the possibility that the dispute deepens further before the year is out.

politics.title: CNN poll: Voters favor Democrats by 8 points as midterm campaign season kicks into gear
politics.dek: With Labor Day marking the unofficial start of general election campaigning, a CNN survey shows Democrats holding a clear generic-ballot lead and a wide enthusiasm edge, as voters signal an appetite for wholesale change in Congress.
politics.author: Amélie Roussel
politics.imageAlt: The U.S. Capitol dome seen against the sky ahead of the 2026 midterm elections

body.text: The week of Labor Day traditionally marks the unofficial start of general election campaigning, and this year that kickoff arrives with Democrats holding a meaningful edge in the fight for Congress. A CNN poll conducted by SSRS in late July found Democrats leading Republicans by 8 points on the generic congressional ballot among registered voters, 47% to 39%, with President Trump's unpopularity and heightened Democratic enthusiasm both weighing on Republicans' chances of holding their majorities in November.

The enthusiasm gap may be just as significant as the topline number. Democrats hold a substantial advantage in overall voter enthusiasm, and among the subset of voters who describe themselves as extremely motivated to vote this fall, that Democratic advantage widens to 20 points. Trump's approval rating, meanwhile, has continued to sag, sitting at roughly 40.6% in a Decision Desk HQ polling average taken around the same time, against a disapproval rating near 57.5%, as voters express frustration over the economy and the ongoing conflict involving Iran.
What we know so far

Beyond the horserace numbers, the poll captured a broader hunger for change in Washington. A majority of voters said Congress would be better off if most of its current members were replaced this fall, and more Americans said the country would be better off (38%) than worse off (33%) if Democrats took control of Congress, with the remainder saying it wouldn't make much difference either way. Among voters who want change, the appetite skews toward younger candidates and new leadership within the Democratic Party more than toward a specific ideological shift, whether leftward or toward the center.

The findings complicate a simple partisan narrative in a few places, too. On the question of which party is doing too much on race and gender issues, Americans were nearly evenly split, with 31% saying Republicans focus too heavily on the topic and 36% saying the same of Democrats. And on corruption, an issue Democrats have tried to spotlight as a midterm message, voters were about evenly divided on which party is more guilty of it, with nearly half saying neither side is meaningfully fighting it.
What it means heading into the fall

With roughly two months now separating the country from Election Day, Republicans face the challenge of overcoming both a generic-ballot deficit and a president whose approval ratings remain underwater, all while defending narrow majorities in both chambers. Democrats, for their part, hold a real advantage in this snapshot, but the same poll's findings on voter appetite for younger leadership and dissatisfaction with the status quo suggest the party's edge may hinge less on enthusiasm for Democrats specifically and more on a broader desire among voters to shake up Washington altogether, a dynamic that could cut in unpredictable directions as individual races take shape this fall.

politics.title: Federal judge rules West Point policy restricting professors' speech is unconstitutional
politics.dek: A ruling in a long-running free speech lawsuit permanently frees civilian faculty at the U.S. Military Academy to speak and write publicly without prior approval, capping a fight that began after Trump ordered service academies to root out 'divisive' ideas.
politics.author: Amélie Roussel
politics.imageAlt: The U.S. Military Academy campus at West Point

body.text: A federal judge has ruled that a West Point policy restricting civilian professors from speaking or writing publicly without prior approval is unconstitutional, delivering a decisive win in a First Amendment lawsuit that has played out over the academy's faculty for the better part of a year. The ruling permits professors at the U.S. Military Academy to comment, publish and speak without first clearing it with department leadership.

The policy at the center of the case dates back to early 2026, when West Point leadership adopted a rule requiring any professor to seek approval from a department head before giving a speech, publishing a paper, or appearing on a podcast. The academy introduced the policy roughly a month after President Trump signed an executive order barring military service academies from what the order described as "promoting, advancing or otherwise inculcating" ideas deemed "un-American" or "divisive."
What we know so far

The case was originally brought by Tim Bakken, West Point's longest-serving law professor, who sued the academy in late 2025 on behalf of all civilian faculty, who make up roughly a third of the school's approximately 700-member teaching staff. Bakken argued the policy violated the First Amendment by effectively censoring viewpoints that might run contrary to positions held by the academy, the Army, the Defense Department, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, or Trump himself. He said he faced retaliation for bringing the suit, including what he described as a disciplinary action stemming from a minor interaction with a mail clerk, and that some colleagues distanced themselves from him over the litigation.

U.S. District Judge Cathy Seibel, a nominee of President George W. Bush, issued an interim ruling in July blocking West Point from enforcing the policy against civilian professors while the case proceeded, and also barred the academy from preventing Bakken from sharing his personal opinions with students. West Point chose not to appeal that interim order, and this week's ruling appears to make that protection more durable, addressing the underlying constitutional question directly rather than leaving the policy merely paused pending further litigation.
Part of a broader pattern

The Bakken case isn't the only free speech fight underway at the academy. A separate lawsuit, filed more recently by another longtime professor, alleges West Point went further still, actually ordering instructors not to teach the scientific consensus on human-caused climate change. That professor's attorney has described his client as a conservative who doesn't take particular ideological issue with Trump, but who believes cadets deserve to be taught accurate information regardless of politics. Together, the cases form part of a wider pattern of legal challenges to how the Trump administration's directives on "divisive" content have been implemented across the nation's service academies, which last winter also saw West Point shut down a number of student clubs organized around gender and minority identity as part of a broader rollback of diversity programming.

politics.title: Rubio tours Latin America's new right-wing allies as Venezuela oil deal draws scrutiny
politics.dek: Secretary of State Marco Rubio is visiting Colombia, Ecuador and Peru this week to court the region's newly elected conservative governments, even as a controversial U.S. deal granting access to Venezuelan oil reserves complicates his message.
politics.author: Amélie Roussel
politics.imageAlt: Secretary of State Marco Rubio meeting with Latin American officials during a regional diplomatic tour

body.text: Secretary of State Marco Rubio kicked off a three-day tour of Latin America on Tuesday, stopping in Colombia, Ecuador and Peru to shore up ties with a wave of newly elected, U.S.-aligned conservative governments across the region. The trip, running September 8 through 10, comes at what Rubio has described as a moment of genuine ideological realignment in the Western Hemisphere, one he's called an "extraordinary achievement" for Washington's regional influence.

The itinerary reflects that shift directly. In Colombia, Rubio met with newly inaugurated right-wing President Abelardo De La Espriella in the coastal city of Barranquilla, with a central focus on formalizing U.S. support for the country's recovery from a devastating 7.4-magnitude earthquake that struck western Colombia in August, killing more than 330 people and causing an estimated $9.6 billion in damage. From there, Rubio travels to Ecuador to meet President Daniel Noboa, and finally to Peru for talks with President Keiko Fujimori, who was inaugurated at the end of July.
What we know so far

Rubio told reporters before departing that the administration hopes to finalize trade agreements with all three countries in the near future, alongside deeper security cooperation on migration and drug trafficking. Notably absent from the itinerary is Venezuela itself, which Rubio said simply couldn't fit into an already condensed week bookended by Labor Day and the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks, though he indicated a visit there would come eventually.

That absence is conspicuous given the backdrop of the trip. Rubio's tour follows closely on the heels of a controversial U.S. deal with Venezuela's interim government, struck in the aftermath of the January operation that removed former President Nicolás Maduro from power. The agreement grants American companies access to an estimated 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan crude oil reserves over the next century, oil fields the administration says had previously been controlled by Chinese, Russian and Iranian interests. Rubio has defended the arrangement as a way to eventually generate revenue for ordinary Venezuelans under a future democratic government, though the deal has reportedly cost him some of the goodwill he once enjoyed among Venezuelans who saw him as a longtime advocate for the country.
A harder line on aid

The trip also underscores a broader shift in how the administration approaches the region. Rubio has been blunt about conditioning U.S. support on cooperation, telling members of Congress earlier this year that "the United States government is not a charity," a marked departure from past approaches to foreign assistance. With Brazil and Mexico now standing as the region's remaining major powers with left-leaning leadership, and with Washington simultaneously tightening pressure on Cuba through an ongoing fuel blockade, Rubio's tour is as much a statement about which governments the U.S. intends to prioritize going forward as it is a routine diplomatic visit.

us.title: The US Just Banned Canadian Dairy, Alcohol, and Motorcycles as the Trade War Keeps Escalating
us.dek: The import bans, taking effect September 29, came hours after Canada's own retaliatory tariffs on $20 billion in US goods kicked in, the latest tit-for-tat in a dispute that's now cast doubt on the future of the USMCA trade agreement.
us.author: David Okafor
us.imageAlt: Prime Minister Mark Carney speaks to journalists in Ottawa amid escalating US-Canada trade tensions
us.metaDescription: The US banned Canadian dairy, alcohol, and motorcycle imports effective September 29, hours after Canada's retaliatory tariffs on $20 billion in US goods began.

body.text: The trade war between the United States and Canada took another sharp turn Tuesday, with Washington announcing new import bans on Canadian alcohol, motorcycles, and dairy products just hours after Ottawa's own retaliatory tariffs on US goods took effect at midnight. The bans, published on the White House's website, are set to take effect September 29.
What We Know So Far

The sequence of escalation is now several rounds deep. The United States imposed 50% tariffs on roughly $20 billion of Canadian goods last month after several rounds of negotiations between the two countries collapsed. Canada responded with its own retaliatory tariffs on US goods, which took effect after midnight Tuesday, prompting Washington's latest countermove: a broad ban on Canadian alcoholic beverages, motorcycles, and dairy products entering the US market entirely.

A US official confirmed that President Trump's pre-existing threat to raise tariffs on Canadian autos from 25% to 50% starting January 1 remains in effect as well, meaning Tuesday's dairy and alcohol bans are layered on top of an already scheduled escalation rather than replacing it.
Diplomatic Channels Are Still Technically Open

Despite the deepening dispute, direct contact between the two governments hasn't been severed entirely. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer has spoken with Dominic LeBlanc, Canada's minister responsible for bilateral US trade, over the past several days, according to a US official, and the two were expected to speak again in the coming days to explore whether an alternative path forward exists. LeBlanc addressed the latest measures directly in a social media post Tuesday night, criticizing the new bans while saying he remained in contact with Greer. He wrote that Canada's first priority remains protecting and supporting Canadian workers, farmers, families, and businesses from what he described as unjustified actions, a framing consistent with Ottawa's position throughout the eighteen-month dispute.
Canada Signals a Broader Strategic Shift

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney used the moment to signal something bigger than a single round of retaliatory measures. In a video posted to YouTube Tuesday, Carney said Canada has everything it needs to pivot and prosper, explicitly urging a further shift away from reliance on the United States as Canada's largest trading partner. He acknowledged that pivot would come at a real cost, but argued that cost doesn't come close to the cost of standing still, language that suggests Ottawa is preparing for a more prolonged period of strained trade relations rather than a quick resolution.
What This Means for the Broader Trade Relationship

The breakdown has widened what was already a significant rift between two countries that have historically been among each other's closest trading allies, and has cast real doubt on the long-term viability of the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement, the trade pact that replaced NAFTA. Beyond Tuesday's specific bans, Ottawa has also moved to shut Canadian products out of large, long-term US government contracts, part of a broader pattern of retaliatory measures extending well beyond the specific goods named in this week's announcement.
What Comes Next

With the new US import bans not taking effect until September 29, both sides technically have a three-week window during which further negotiation, or further escalation, remains possible. Whether the renewed Greer-LeBlanc contact produces any actual breakthrough, or whether the dispute continues following the same pattern of tariff and countertariff that's defined the relationship for the past year and a half, is likely to become clearer well before the bans formally take hold at the end of the month.

us.title: Florida Just Ran Its Largest Child Recovery Operation Ever. It Found 163 Kids.
us.dek: Operation Statewide Shield brought together local, state, and federal agencies over five days, recovering children from six other US states, one territory, and a dozen foreign countries, with three arrests made and more expected.
us.author: David Okafor
us.imageAlt: Florida law enforcement officials at a press conference announcing the results of Operation Statewide Shield
us.metaDescription: Florida's Operation Statewide Shield recovered 163 missing children in five days, the largest child-recovery operation in state history, officials announced.

body.text: Florida officials announced late last month that a five-day, multi-agency operation had recovered 163 missing children, the largest operation of its kind in the state's history and, according to the agencies involved, one of the largest child-recovery efforts ever conducted in the United States. Attorney General James Uthmeier and Florida Department of Law Enforcement Commissioner Mark Glass announced the results of Operation Statewide Shield on August 25, describing a coordinated effort that reached well beyond Florida's own borders.
What We Know So Far

The recovered children ranged in age from just 2 months to 17 years old. Regional task forces conducted sub-operations across seven areas of the state: 46 children were recovered in the Tampa Bay region, 41 in Miami, 32 in Jacksonville, 21 in Orlando, 12 in Fort Myers, 8 in Pensacola, and 3 in Tallahassee. The search extended beyond Florida entirely, with children also located across six other US states, Puerto Rico, and twelve foreign countries, including Brazil, Canada, Colombia, Mexico, Spain, and Taiwan.

Officials said many of the children recovered had experienced abuse, neglect, exploitation, or exposure to other criminal activity, including human trafficking. Florida prosecutor Rita Peters, who served as Special Counsel for Human Trafficking on the operation, noted the recovered children also included runaways, indicating the effort wasn't narrowly focused on a single trafficking network but cast a genuinely wide net across different categories of missing and at-risk youth.
How the Operation Actually Worked

The Florida Department of Law Enforcement led the investigation, building its framework using strategies developed during earlier federal law enforcement initiatives, including operations known internally as Dragon Eye and Home for the Holidays. Once located, recovered children were transported to specialized hubs offering medical care, psychological support, and broader child welfare services, rather than being processed through a single generic intake point.

Attorney General Uthmeier said in a statement that many of the children involved had been victimized by people who prey on the most vulnerable, and credited the law enforcement officers and victim advocates involved with giving the recovered children hope and a second chance. Three arrests were made in connection with the operation as of the August 25 announcement, with officials indicating additional charges were expected as investigations connected to the sweep continued.
Putting the Numbers in Context

Florida's operation is part of a broader, ongoing pattern of similar law enforcement efforts nationally. The US Marshals Service, which operates a dedicated Missing Child Unit, has located or recovered more than 4,561 missing children since receiving enhanced legal authority for that work in 2015, recovering missing children in roughly 67% of cases the agency receives, with 61% of those recoveries happening within the first seven days. Separately, a nationwide effort known as Operation Soteria Shield, run in coordination with the FBI and the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children, rescued 89 children and led to 276 arrests in an April 2026 sweep focused specifically on online child sexual exploitation.
What Comes Next

Law enforcement agencies involved in Operation Statewide Shield have said investigations connected to the sweep remain open, and authorities have not yet publicly identified all individuals believed to be leading the exploitation networks the operation uncovered. For families and community members concerned about a child's safety, the Childhelp National Child Abuse Hotline, reachable at 1-800-4-A-Child, remains available around the clock for confidential guidance, with officials emphasizing that community vigilance continues to play a genuine role in identifying children who need help.

us.title: The Trump Administration Just Told Ford Its Chinese Partnerships Are a Security Risk. Ford Pushed Back Hard.
us.dek: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Ford's dealings with battery maker CATL and automakers Geely and BYD raise 'profound concern,' while Ford called the letter a 'wrongheaded attempt to capture headlines.'
us.author: David Okafor
us.imageAlt: Ford's battery manufacturing plant in Marshall, Michigan, where the automaker licenses technology from China's CATL
us.metaDescription: The Trump administration criticized Ford's ties to Chinese firms CATL, Geely, and BYD over security concerns; Ford called the letter misleading.

body.text: The Trump administration escalated its scrutiny of Ford Motor Company's ties to Chinese manufacturers this week, with US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy sending CEO Jim Farley a letter warning that the automaker's partnerships with Chinese battery maker CATL and automakers Geely and BYD raise what he called profound concern for national security. The letter, dated late last week and made public Tuesday, urges Ford to reconsider the scope of those relationships.
What We Know So Far

Duffy's central target is Ford's battery plant in Marshall, Michigan, where the company produces lithium-iron-phosphate battery cells using licensed technology from CATL. The Department of Transportation said it was deeply alarmed by that arrangement, arguing that prioritizing imported Chinese technical expertise and operational know-how, even in a scaled-back capacity, challenges the spirit of American national and economic security and supply-chain independence policy. Duffy specifically noted that CATL sits on the Pentagon's list of companies the US government has accused of ties to China's military, a designation the Department of Defense applied in January 2025, before Trump took office.

The letter didn't stop at the CATL relationship. Duffy also criticized Ford's joint venture with Chinese automaker Geely in Spain, writing that it helps strategic adversaries secure a vital foothold in Western markets. He raised separate concerns about Ford's ongoing talks with China's BYD over hybrid vehicle components, warning those discussions could lead to further embedding subsidized foreign technology into Ford's core supply chains.
A Timeline Dispute Over the Lincoln Nautilus

One specific product decision drew particularly pointed criticism. Ford has planned to move production of the Lincoln Nautilus SUV from China to the United States, but not until 2030. Duffy called that timeline unacceptable, writing it leaves an unacceptable, multi-year window of reliance on Chinese manufacturing for a vehicle sold to American consumers.
Ford's Response

Ford didn't accept the criticism quietly. In a statement, the company called Duffy's letter a wrongheaded attempt to capture headlines, and pushed back on the underlying premise directly, arguing that while others continue importing Chinese batteries, Ford is actually investing to build batteries here in America. The company emphasized that it owns the Marshall, Michigan, facility outright, framing its arrangement with CATL as a licensing relationship for specific battery technology rather than the kind of deeper operational dependence Duffy's letter implied.
Congress Has Been Watching This Relationship Too

The administration's letter adds to scrutiny Ford has already faced from Capitol Hill over its China partnerships. Representative John Moolenaar of Michigan, who chairs the House Select Committee on China, has previously criticized Ford's Geely joint venture specifically, arguing the partnership will further enable China's decimation of auto markets in Europe. That kind of bipartisan-adjacent congressional attention suggests Ford's Chinese manufacturing relationships were already a live political issue well before Duffy's letter became public this week.
The Bigger Picture Behind the Dispute

The confrontation arrives amid broader, escalating US-China trade and technology tensions that have touched nearly every major American industry with Chinese manufacturing ties this year. For the auto industry specifically, Chinese battery technology has become genuinely difficult to avoid entirely, CATL is one of the world's largest battery manufacturers and a major supplier across the global EV industry, meaning US automakers face real trade-offs between accessing competitive battery technology and satisfying increasingly assertive national security concerns coming out of Washington.
What Happens Next

Neither Duffy's letter nor Ford's public rebuttal indicates any immediate regulatory action forcing changes to the automaker's Chinese partnerships. For now, the dispute remains a public war of words between a cabinet official and one of America's largest automakers rather than a formal enforcement action, though the letter's public release and its overlap with existing congressional scrutiny suggest this particular fight over Ford's supply chain is unlikely to fade quickly, especially as the broader US-China trade relationship continues to generate friction across other industries simultaneously.

us.title: Trump awards 'Man in the Red Bandana' the Medal of Freedom ahead of 9/11's 25th anniversary
us.dek: President Trump posthumously honored Welles Crowther, the 24-year-old equities trader credited with saving 18 lives in the World Trade Center's South Tower, as the country prepares to mark a quarter-century since the September 11 attacks.
us.author: David Okafor
us.imageAlt: A steel beam from the World Trade Center's South Tower on display in Washington, D.C., ahead of the 25th anniversary of 9/11

body.text: Twenty-five years after the September 11 attacks, one of that day's quiet acts of heroism received the nation's highest civilian honor. President Trump posthumously awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom to Welles Crowther, a 24-year-old equities trader and volunteer firefighter remembered as the "Man in the Red Bandana," during a White House commemoration event on the Ellipse on Tuesday, just days before Friday's 25th anniversary of the attacks.

Crowther worked on the 104th floor of the World Trade Center's South Tower when the building was struck. Rather than making his way to safety, he located a still-passable stairwell and used it to reach the 78th floor, where survivors trapped amid fire, smoke and debris believed they had no way out. According to accounts from the 9/11 Memorial & Museum, Crowther, his face covered by a red bandana, calmed the group, helped extinguish nearby flames, and began leading them down the stairs. He made repeated trips back up to guide others to safety before the tower collapsed, ultimately saving an estimated 18 people before he was killed in the lobby.
What we know so far

Trump presented the medal to Crowther's mother, Alison, and sister, Paige, who accepted it on his behalf during a ceremony organized alongside the Tunnel to Towers Foundation. The event, part of the foundation's "Steel Across America" tour, featured a 21-foot, 16,900-pound steel beam recovered from the South Tower's wreckage, which has been carried across the country in the weeks leading up to the anniversary. "This means the world to me, my daughters, Paige and Honor, and our entire family," Alison Crowther said. "This will be treasured for generations to come."

Trump also honored New York City firefighter Jeffrey Palazzo, who died in the attacks, announcing that a new U.S. Coast Guard cutter would be named in his honor. In remarks to the crowd of first responders, Gold Star families and Tunnel to Towers supporters, Trump described the roughly 3,000 lives lost across the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and aboard United Flight 93, calling the anniversary a chance to reaffirm what he called "the sacred vow we made a quarter of a century ago: We will never forget."
What comes next

Commemoration events are set to continue through the anniversary itself on Friday, September 11, when Trump is expected to attend a ceremony at the Pentagon. Crowther's legacy has already extended well beyond the medal ceremony: his family established the Red Bandana Project, a social and emotional learning curriculum now used in schools to teach the kind of courage and compassion he showed in his final hour. As the country marks 25 years since the attacks, officials and families alike have framed this year's commemorations as both a remembrance of the lives lost and a reminder, for a generation of Americans born after 2001, of what happened that morning and why the country continues to gather each September to honor it.

sports.title: UMass's Stunning Upset of Rutgers Reshapes This Rebuilding Season!
sports.dek: Coming off a winless 2025 season and a 16-game losing streak, UMass shocked Rutgers as 29.5-point underdogs, pulling off the biggest FBS point-spread upset in years and forcing a reset of expectations for both programs.
sports.author: Tomás Herrera
sports.imageAlt: UMass Minutemen players celebrating during their upset win over Rutgers

body.text: Nobody outside the UMass locker room saw this coming, and honestly, most people inside it probably didn't either. The Minutemen opened the 2026 college football season as 29.5-point underdogs at Rutgers, a program that had gone winless the year before and hadn't beaten an FBS opponent since 2023. What happened instead, a 37-21 win over the Scarlet Knights, instantly became one of the biggest point-spread upsets the sport has seen in years, and it's already forcing a rethink of what a rebuilding program can accomplish in a single offseason.

The numbers behind the shock make it even harder to believe. UMass had lost 16 straight games, the longest active losing streak in the FBS, and hadn't tasted victory at all since beating FCS opponent Wagner back in October 2024, a stretch of 677 days. Rutgers, meanwhile, had actually paid UMass a reported $1.55 million just to make the trip to New Jersey, a so-called "paycheck game" typically scheduled by power programs expecting an easy win. Instead, it became the second-most expensive loss of its kind in the sport's history.
What we know so far

UMass quarterback William "Pop" Watson III, a transfer from Virginia Tech, was nearly flawless, completing 19 of 22 passes for 197 yards and three touchdowns while adding 40 rushing yards on the ground. He spread the ball across seven different receivers and led the Minutemen to scores on seven of their ten offensive drives, building a 24-7 halftime lead, the program's first at the break against a power-conference opponent since a 2017 game against Mississippi State. Curtis Kimmons IV added a late touchdown run to push the lead to 37-14 before Rutgers managed a garbage-time score.

The Minutemen's defense was every bit as important as their offense. UMass forced five turnovers, including three interceptions off Rutgers quarterback Dylan Lonergan, marking the program's best turnover performance since 2022. Rutgers actually out-gained UMass in total yardage, 349 to 397 isn't the disparity it might seem, but four turnovers and a miserable 3-of-11 mark on third-down conversions doomed the Scarlet Knights despite a strong individual outing from wide receiver KJ Duff, who caught three touchdown passes.
A program remade almost overnight

What makes UMass's turnaround especially notable is how completely the roster changed in a single offseason. The Minutemen brought in 56 new players, including 30 transfers and 26 true freshmen, an overhaul aimed at fixing an offense that averaged just 11.1 points per game in 2025, the worst mark in the entire FBS. Head coach Joe Harasymiak, in his first game leading the program, got a particularly sweet measure of vindication, since he spent the previous three seasons as Rutgers' own defensive coordinator before taking the UMass job.

Rutgers head coach Greg Schiano didn't mince words afterward, telling reporters plainly that his team had been outcoached and outplayed. For UMass, the win is still just one game in a 12-game season, and nobody is ready to call this a finished turnaround. But for a program that entered the year with the lowest expectations in the country, a single Thursday night in Piscataway was enough to force rivals, bettors and college football fans everywhere to reconsider exactly what this UMass team might be capable of before the season is through.

sports.title: Brandon Graham Retires for Good, Closing Out His Eagles Legacy
sports.dek: The two-time Super Bowl champion and Eagles' all-time leader in games played is stepping away for the second and final time, one day before Philadelphia's 2026 season opener, closing out a career defined by loyalty, grit and one unforgettable Super Bowl strip-sack.
sports.author: Tomás Herrera
sports.imageAlt: Brandon Graham holding the Lombardi Trophy during his Philadelphia Eagles retirement announcement

body.text: Brandon Graham is done, for real this time. The Philadelphia Eagles defensive end announced Tuesday, just one day before the team's 2026 season opener against Washington, that he is officially retiring from the NFL after a career that spans parts of two decades and includes two Super Bowl championships, all of them earned wearing the same midnight green jersey.

It's the second time Graham has walked away. He first retired in March 2025 in an emotional, tear-filled press conference after 15 seasons, only to come out of retirement roughly six months later to rejoin a 5-2 Eagles team chasing another title. This time, at 38 years old, he's making it official for good. "I'm officially done. Y'all hearing it from me first," Graham told reporters, before immediately shifting the spotlight away from himself and onto the teammates he's leaving behind.
What we know so far

Graham's numbers tell the story of remarkable consistency and loyalty in a league where neither is common. Drafted 13th overall out of Michigan in 2010, he spent his entire career with the Eagles, retiring as the franchise's all-time leader in both games played, 206, and seasons played, ahead of Eagles legends like Jason Kelce and Fletcher Cox. He finishes third in franchise history in career sacks and earned a lone Pro Bowl selection in 2022, a recognition that came unusually late for a player of his caliber, a fact many Eagles fans have long argued undersold his impact.

No single moment defines Graham's legacy more than his strip-sack of Tom Brady in Super Bowl LII, a play that helped seal the Eagles' first Super Bowl title in franchise history. He added a second ring in Super Bowl LIX, closing out that game and what he thought at the time was his final season while playing through a ruptured left triceps, a fitting encapsulation of a career built on toughness and refusing to quit.
Tributes pour in

The reaction from teammates and the organization was immediate and heartfelt. Longtime teammate Lane Johnson called Graham a "brother for life" on social media, reflecting on years of competing against each other daily in practice. Eagles owner Jeffrey Lurie previously described Graham as the embodiment of everything the franchise wants in a player, both on and off the field. Even in this latest, final announcement, Graham stayed focused on what's ahead for the team rather than dwelling on his own exit, praising young defensive lineman Jordan Davis as someone ready to carry the Eagles' defense forward.

For a city that has watched Graham grow from an unproven first-round pick into one of the most beloved players in franchise history, his retirement closes out an era. He becomes the oldest player in Eagles history to record a sack, a distinction he added just last season during his brief return. Whatever comes next for Graham, Philadelphia's football fans will remember him as the player who helped deliver two championships and never stopped fighting for one more.

sports.title: Seahawks Host Patriots Tonight in NFL Season's Super Bowl LX Rematch
sports.dek: The defending champion Seattle Seahawks open their title defense at Lumen Field tonight against the very team they beat in February, with Sam Darnold and Drake Maye renewing their rivalry in the league's marquee season opener.
sports.author: Tomás Herrera
sports.imageAlt: Lumen Field in Seattle prepared for the 2026 NFL season opener

body.text: The wait is finally over. The 2026 NFL season kicks off tonight at Lumen Field, where the defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks host the New England Patriots in a rematch of February's Super Bowl LX, one of only a handful of times in league history that the two participants from the previous season's championship game have met again in Week 1. Kickoff is set for 8:20 p.m. ET, broadcast nationally on NBC with Jim Nantz and Cris Collinsworth calling the action.

The scheduling is unusual by design. This is a Wednesday game rather than the league's typical Thursday-night opener, a shift made to clear room for the NFL's first-ever regular-season game in Melbourne, Australia, which follows the next night when the Los Angeles Rams face the San Francisco 49ers. History favors the champs in this particular spot: teams that have opened a season as the reigning Super Bowl winner have gone a combined 16-5 in that game since 2004.
What we know so far

Both teams enter the rematch with essentially the rosters that got them to Santa Clara in February, and both finished last season 14-3. Seattle quarterback Sam Darnold, coming off a career-reviving campaign that ended in a championship, threw for 4,048 yards, 25 touchdowns and 14 interceptions a season ago while completing 67.7% of his passes. He'll lean once again on receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba, who caught 119 passes for nearly 1,800 yards and 10 touchdowns in 2025, making him one of the league's most productive pass catchers.

On the other sideline, Drake Maye enters his second full season as New England's starter looking to prove last season's run to the Super Bowl was no fluke, even after a difficult performance in that loss to Seattle. The Patriots' offense was actually the league's most efficient through the air last year, posting the NFL's highest completion percentage and catch rate, numbers that suggest Maye and his receiving corps have real firepower even after falling short in February.
What to watch for

Oddsmakers have installed Seattle as a 3.5-point favorite at home, with the total set at 44.5 points, a relatively modest number for two teams that both finished among the league's better offenses a year ago. Both defenses were also stout in 2025, which suggests tonight's opener could hinge less on which offense explodes and more on which team wins the turnover battle and forces the other into mistakes. Given how close last season's Super Bowl ended up being, a similarly tight, hard-fought rematch wouldn't be a surprise.

Beyond tonight's opener, Week 1 continues Thursday with the Rams-49ers game in Australia before the rest of the league's schedule unfolds over the weekend, including a Monday night doubleheader featuring the Giants at the Cowboys and the Chiefs at the Broncos. But all eyes start in Seattle tonight, where the road to Super Bowl LXI in February effectively begins with a rematch of how last season ended.

sports.title: Tiafoe Pulls Off Stunning Two-Set Comeback to Reach US Open Semi
sports.dek: Down two sets to unseeded Alex Michelsen, Tiafoe rallied to book his third career US Open semifinal appearance, a comeback so rare that the last man to pull one off at the tournament was Roger Federer.
sports.author: Tomás Herrera
sports.imageAlt: Frances Tiafoe celebrating during his comeback quarterfinal win at the US Open

body.text: Frances Tiafoe has made a habit of thriving under pressure at his home Grand Slam, and Tuesday's quarterfinal against fellow American Alex Michelsen may have been the wildest example yet. Down two sets to the unseeded Michelsen, the 11th-seeded Tiafoe fought back to win in five, punching his ticket to the US Open semifinals for the third time in his career with a comeback that instantly became one of the signature moments of this year's tournament.

The scale of the achievement is best understood by the company it puts him in. According to tournament historians, the last men's player to come back from two sets down to win a US Open quarterfinal was Roger Federer, underlining just how rarely a comeback of this magnitude happens on tennis's biggest American stage. Michelsen, playing with nothing to lose against a far more experienced opponent, came out aggressive and built a commanding lead before Tiafoe found his rhythm and clawed his way back into the match.
What we know so far

Tiafoe's win came on a jam-packed quarterfinal day at Flushing Meadows that produced two other American storylines. Third-seeded Jessica Pegula outlasted fellow American Emma Navarro in three sets, 3-6, 6-4, 6-3, to reach the semifinals, while defending women's champion Aryna Sabalenka survived a three-set thriller of her own against Linda Noskova, winning a tense final-set tiebreaker 7-6(1), 3-6, 7-6(7) to keep her bid for a US Open three-peat alive.

The day's other headline came earlier, when China's Qinwen Zheng pulled off a similarly improbable comeback of her own, rallying from 0-5 down in the first set to upset Iga Świątek in straight sets, 7-5, 6-3. It marked the second consecutive match in which Zheng erased a 0-5 deficit to win a set, a stretch of resilience that has quickly become one of the tournament's most talked-about storylines heading into the final rounds.
What comes next

Tiafoe's win sets up a semifinal appearance that will test whether Tuesday's dramatic escape leaves him with enough in the tank for the tournament's final stretch, a familiar challenge for a player who has built a reputation for producing his best tennis in New York's electric night sessions. With Pegula and Sabalenka both through as well, and the men's and women's draws both still carrying multiple American contenders, the 2026 US Open is shaping up as one of the more dramatic and competitive editions of the tournament in recent memory heading into the semifinal round.

sports.title: Patriots Make Gonzalez NFL's Highest-Paid Cornerback in History
sports.dek: New England locked up its 24-year-old All-Pro cornerback on a four-year, $135 million extension just 48 hours before kicking off the 2026 season against Seattle, ending months of tense contract talks in dramatic fashion.
sports.author: Tomás Herrera
sports.imageAlt: New England Patriots cornerback Christian Gonzalez on the field before a game

body.text: For months, a contract standoff between the New England Patriots and star cornerback Christian Gonzalez hung over the team's preparations for a season opener against the Seattle Seahawks. That cloud finally lifted Monday night, when the two sides agreed to a four-year, $135 million extension that includes $102 million in guaranteed money, making Gonzalez the highest-paid cornerback in NFL history just two days before kickoff.

The deal, worth $33.75 million annually in new-money average, edges out the previous record set by Seattle's own Devon Witherspoon, who had signed a $33 million-per-year extension with the Seahawks just last month. According to details of the contract, Gonzalez received a $33 million signing bonus, along with fully guaranteed base salaries for both 2026 and 2027, giving the 24-year-old long-term financial security through the 2031 season.
What we know so far

Negotiations had reportedly gone cold at points over the summer, with disagreements over contract language and guarantee structures dragging talks into what one NFL insider described as the eleventh hour. The Patriots had already exercised Gonzalez's fifth-year option earlier in the year, locking him in through 2027 on a smaller salary, but that arrangement left both sides with real financial incentive to get a longer-term deal done before the season began, especially given Gonzalez's standing as one of the league's best young defensive backs.

The 17th overall pick in the 2023 draft out of Oregon, Gonzalez has quickly developed into a cornerstone of New England's defense, earning Second-Team All-Pro honors in 2024 and a Pro Bowl selection last season. He was especially prominent during the Patriots' surprise run to Super Bowl LX, recording an interception, a sack and seven pass breakups across four playoff games, including a game-clinching interception in the AFC Championship that helped send New England to the title game.
Timing that couldn't be better

Getting the deal finalized before Wednesday night's opener carried real stakes beyond just the money. Gonzalez had skipped New England's voluntary offseason workouts amid the contract dispute, though he did attend the team's mandatory minicamp in June, and reports suggested growing concern that an unresolved situation could have led to Gonzalez sitting out the marquee Super Bowl rematch against Seattle rather than risk injury on an expiring, cheaper contract. With the extension now signed, New England enters its title defense with its top cornerback fully committed and available, removing what had become one of the more significant storylines of the team's offseason.
